binders: An arbitrary type Omega equipped with a measurable-space structure.
An arbitrary finite type I of indices.
A family Bad assigning an arbitrary subset Bad(i) of Omega to each i in I.
hypotheses: For every index i in I, the real conversion (mu(Bad(i))).toReal is at most q.
conclusions: The real conversion of the measure of the union of all Bad(i) is at most the sum, over all i in I, of the real conversions of mu(Bad(i)).
That same finite sum is at most the real cardinality of I multiplied by q.
mathematical_definitions: Write m(A) = (mu(A)).toReal for the real-valued conversion used by the proposition.
Write U = union over i in I of Bad(i).
Write S = sum over i in I of m(Bad(i)) and n = |I|.
translation.proposition_plain_english: For every measure mu, every finite family of subsets Bad(i), and every real q, if each converted measure m(Bad(i)) is at most q, then both m(union over i of Bad(i)) <= sum over i of m(Bad(i)) and sum over i of m(Bad(i)) <= |I| q. Equivalently, the proposition explicitly asserts the chain m(union over i of Bad(i)) <= sum over i of m(Bad(i)) <= |I| q as two conjunctive inequalities.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The index type is finite; the statement does not cover an infinite or countable family.
The ambient measure is arbitrary and is not assumed to be a probability measure.
No measurability hypothesis is imposed on the individual sets Bad(i) or stated for their union.

The proposition uses (mu(A)).toReal. If mu(A) is infinite, extended nonnegative infinity is not preserved as a real infinity, so this expression does not encode the usual extended-real measure value; no finiteness assumptions are present to rule this out.

The common bound q is an arbitrary real number, with no explicit nonnegativity or unit-interval constraint. For a nonempty family, a negative q makes the premise impossible because converted measure values are nonnegative, so that case is vacuous.
If the finite index type is empty, the pointwise premise is vacuous; the union and sum are empty and the cardinality factor is zero.
The statement contains only the two numerical inequalities. It does not encode independence, disjointness, identical distributions, or any other structural relationship among the sets.
